title: Trunk-based development: merge before it is finished
summary: Branches live hours, not weeks. Ship an unfinished feature safely behind a flag, keep main always releasable, and see why this model has almost no merge conflicts.
mental_model: Merge conflicts are a function of time apart, not of team size. Trunk-based development attacks the time: everyone merges to main daily, and unfinished work hides behind a flag rather than behind a branch.

commit.message: Add controller with a feature flag module

steps.title: Day one: add the flag, off by default
steps.why: The first commit of any large change adds a flag that turns it off. It is safe to merge immediately because it changes nothing at runtime — and merging immediately is the entire point.

actions.run: git commit -q -m "Add auto_dosing feature flag, off by default"

steps.expect: Merged and the branch already deleted — it lived about four minutes.

steps.title: Meanwhile a colleague edits the same file
steps.why: In a branch-per-feature model this is where the conflict is born. Here they merge within the hour, so the two changes never drift apart.

commit.message: Add ph_alerts flag, on by default

steps.expect: Their change is a clean addition next to yours.

steps.title: Day two: pull first, then work
steps.why: `pull --rebase` keeps your work on top of theirs with no merge commit. Doing it at the start of every session is what keeps trunk-based development conflict-free.

actions.run: git commit -q -m "Add dosing schedule behind the auto_dosing flag"

steps.expect: Half-finished code on main, doing nothing, because the flag is off.

verify.label: unfinished work is merged to main daily

steps.title: Prove main is still releasable
steps.why: The new module is inert: with the flag off, `next_dose_time` returns None and nothing calls into it. That property is what makes merging incomplete work honest rather than reckless.
steps.expect: None — the code is present and dormant.

steps.title: Day three: finish it and flip the flag
steps.why: The feature becomes live in a one-line commit, entirely separate from the code that implements it. If it misbehaves in production, the revert is that one line — no code rollback, no redeploy of the previous build.
commands: sh -c 'python -c "import importlib, schedule, flags; importlib.reload(flags); importlib.reload(schedule); print(schedule.next_dose_time(0))"'

verify.label: the feature was enabled by a one-line commit

steps.title: Roll back without touching code
steps.why: Reverting the flag commit disables the feature instantly. Compare with reverting a merged feature branch, which touches every file it added and often conflicts.
steps.expect: One file, two lines — the smallest possible production rollback.

verify.label: the rollback touched only the flag file

steps.title: Look at what history looks like
steps.why: A straight line of small commits, no merge commits, no branches older than a day. `git bisect` works perfectly on this shape, and so does reading it.

verify.label: no merge commits at all — every branch fast-forwarded
history is a straight line: branches lived hours and fast-forwarded
unfinished work shipped to main behind a flag
the feature is currently off, having been rolled back by reverting one line
the rollback did not touch any feature code
no feature branches are left lying around

pitfalls: Trunk-based only works with a test suite you trust and a flag mechanism. Without them, merging unfinished work is exactly as reckless as it sounds.
Flags accumulate. Delete each one within a release or two of shipping, or the codebase becomes a maze of dead branches in the code itself.
`git pull --rebase` at the start of every session is the discipline that avoids conflicts. Set `pull.rebase true` and stop thinking about it.
A branch that lives more than a day or two has stopped being trunk-based, whatever the team calls its process.
cheatsheet: start every session on top of everyone else's work
roll back a feature without touching its code
should be empty in this model
